transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Well... my daughter thought I should come. I guess I just... I feel like I'm always up and moving around. Even on a quiet day, I'm just sort of bouncing from checking my garden club list to looking in my knitting bag, and then over to some travel papers... usually before I've really finished with any of them.
Have you always been this way since childhood, or is this something that's gotten worse recently?

Well... I suppose it's always been this way. It's not really new. Um... even back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my mother that I was... well, bright, but scattered. I was always losing my papers and... talking out of turn, I guess. Wiggling in my seat before I even finished my work. So... yes. It's been a long time.

Have there been times in your life when you felt exceptionally happy or energetic for several days or longer, where you needed much less sleep than usual but still felt rested, and during those times did you feel like you could do things that were unusually ambitious or risky for you?
Um... no. I don't think so. I mean, I've always needed my regular sleep. And I wouldn't say I do... risky things. I'm just... busy, I guess. Not like what you're describing.

When you're working on something that interests you, like your gardening club or knitting, are you able to stick with it and finish what you started, or do you find yourself getting distracted and moving on to something else?

Well... I suppose I get distracted. Even with things I care about. Like... if I'm at a planning meeting for the garden club, or just trying to read the church bulletin... I might start out listening or reading just fine. But then, after a bit... I'll realize I've missed half of what was said. Or printed. I just... lose track, I guess.
When you're managing your daily responsibilities—like paying bills, organizing your home, or keeping track of appointments—do you find that challenging? Do things tend to pile up or get disorganized?

Yes, it... it can be difficult. I suppose things do pile up a bit. Um... right now, I have piles all over the kitchen table. Papers for my dance class, knitting patterns, garden club events, information about trips... it just sits there. And I... I look at it all and I can't always figure out what needs to be done first. So it just stays piled up.
Do you find yourself doing things without thinking first? For example, interrupting people, spending money impulsively, or acting on urges right away without considering the consequences?

Well... I don't know about spending money or... acting on urges. But... my husband does say I cut him off. Before he finishes talking. And... I suppose I do it at the garden club planning meetings, too. It's just... if I don't say what I'm thinking right then, I'm afraid I'll forget it entirely. So I just... say it.

When you're sitting still—say, at dinner with your family or during a movie—do you feel physically restless or fidgety? Do you find yourself tapping your fingers, bouncing your leg, or needing to get up and move around?

Well... I suppose so. If I'm sitting in a meeting, or... even just watching television... I guess I do tend to tap my foot. Or I'll be rubbing my fingers together. Just... fussing with whatever happens to be in my lap. I don't really think much of it, but... yes, I suppose I do that.
When you think back to your earliest school years—say, first or second grade—were you already having trouble paying attention and sitting still, or did these difficulties start later on?

Well... yes. I suppose it's always been this way. Um... I remember my mother saying the teachers thought I was... bright, I guess. But... scattered. They said I was always losing my school papers. And... well, talking out of turn. Wiggling around in my seat instead of finishing my assignments. So... yes, it started early.
Have these difficulties with attention and fidgeting caused real problems for you—like affecting your work, your relationships, or your ability to manage things at home?

Well... yes, I suppose it has. Um... it's caused some strain. Mostly at home, I guess. And... well, at the community center. My husband gets frustrated, and... the other volunteers, too. They just... feel like they can't count on me to keep the plans straight. Not unless someone is checking up behind me. So... yes, it does cause problems.

Differential includes ADHD, generalized anxiety disorder, depressive episode with agitation, bipolar disorder, and organic causes. final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity beginning in early childhood (grade school), with clear functional impairment in home, work, and social settings. Core ADHD symptoms include: difficulty sustaining attention (loses track during meetings/reading), easy distractibility, disorganization (papers piling up, unable to prioritize), physical restlessness (tapping foot, fidgeting), impulsivity (interrupting, speaking without thinking), and difficulty with task completion. Onset prior to age 12 is well-established. The absence of manic/hypomanic episodes rules out bipolar disorder. The constellation of symptoms and chronic course since childhood is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Combined Presentation (or predominantly inattentive with hyperactive features).
